## Looking for Shy Trump Supporters

Are Trump supporters more likely to misreport their views? How would we show evidence for/against this claim?

## Looking for Shy Trump Supporters

Pew Research @pewresearch_shytrump used a survey experiment to look at the effects of phone vs. online polls on supporting Trump/Trump admin policies.

![](../images/pew_shytrump_headline.png){fig-align="center"}

### Looking for Shy Trump Supporters

Pew's Methodology:

-   Randomly assign respondents to answer the same 27 questions by phone (n=1,778) or online (n=2,066)
-   Compare average support across different survey modes to look for evidence of social desirability bias.

### Looking for Shy Trump Supporters

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}
-   There's a small difference in Trump support across survey modes. But the authors say is is *not statistically significant*.

-   There are some statistically significant differences, but they don't all go in the direction one would expect.
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../images/PM.03.30.2017_mode.effects-00-05.webp){fig-align="center" width="60%"}
:::
::::::

### Looking for Shy Trump Supporters

So what does this mean, and how do we know it?

![](../images/pew_shytrump.png){fig-align="center"}

### Central Limit Theorem and sampling distributions

Under the Central Limit Theorem, we know that the sampling distribution of a sample mean:

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size: 50%;"}
1.  Will be approximately normal distributed.
2.  Will be centered around the population mean.
3.  Will have a standard deviation (standard error) of $\sqrt{\frac{s^2}{n}}$
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../images/sampling_distribution.svg){fig-align="center" width="60%"}
:::
::::::

### Central Limit Theorem and sampling distributions

We can use this knowledge to quantify how much uncertainty we have around a single sample mean.

![](../images/norm_colored.png){fig-align="center"}

### Linear combinations of random normal variables

Moreover: **linear combinations (addition/subtraction) of random normal variables are themselves normally distributed.**

### Linear combinations of random normal variables

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| layout-ncol: 4
n<-10000
x1<-rnorm(n, mean=1.5, sd=2)
x2<-rnorm(n, mean=4, sd=3)
plot(density(x1 + x2), 
     main ='Summing')
plot(density(x1 - x2), 
     main='Differencing')
plot(density(x1*3 + x2*1.5), 
     main = "Summing with multiplication by a constant")
plot(density(x1 * x2), 
     main ='Multiplying two random normal variables')



```

### Sampling distributions of a difference {auto-animate="true" auto-animate-easing="ease-in-out"}

We can also make inferences about the difference between two sampling distributions using the same basic logic we used to build a confidence interval around a single estimate.

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}


distFunc<-function(mean, sd){
  x <- seq(from = mean - 5*sd, to = mean + 5*sd, by = .001)
  res <- data.frame(x = x, y = dnorm(x, mean = mean, sd = sd))
  return(res)
}

df1<-distFunc(mean = 0, sd = 1)
df2<-distFunc(mean = 5, sd = 1)



plt<-ggplot(df1, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_line() +
  geom_line(aes(x=df2$x, y=df2$y), lty=2) +
  
  labs(title = "Two groups with different means",
       x = "", y = "Density") 


ggsave(plt, file='../images/two_means.png')


```

![](../images/two_means.png)
:::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}




df3<-distFunc(mean = -5, sd = 0.12)


plt<-ggplot(df3, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_line() +
  
  labs(title = "Group 2 - Group 1",
       x = "", y = "Density") 

ggsave(plt, file='../images/difference_of_means.png')


```

::: {data-id="difference_plot"}
![](../images/difference_of_means.png)
:::

::::::

### Confidence intervals for a difference {auto-animate="true" auto-animate-easing="ease-in-out"}

To get a confidence interval, we just need to find the variance for this sampling distribution.

::: {data-id="difference_plot"}
![](../images/difference_of_means.png){fig-align="center", width="60%"}
:::

### Confidence intervals for a difference

The standard error of the difference between two means is just a weighted combination of their respective variances:

$$
\text{SE}_{\bar{y}_{a} - \bar{y}_{b}} =  \sqrt{\frac{s^2_a}{n_a} + \frac{s^2_b}{n_b}}
$$

::: fragment
For example: if $s_a^2 = 10$, $n_a=100$ and $s_b^2 = 20$, $b_2 = 100$, then:

$$
\text{SE}(\bar{y}_1 - \bar{y}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{10}{100} + \frac{20}{100}} = 0.55
$$
:::

### Confidence intervals for a difference

In Pew's study:

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}
-   Phone respondents had 42% approval for Trump at a sample size of 1,778.
-   Web respondents had 44% approval for Trump at a sample size of 2,066.
-   Pew reports the sample variances as: $s^2_{\text{phone}} = 0.244$ and $s^2_{\text{web}} = 0.246$
:::

### Confidence intervals for a difference

$$\bar{y}_{\text{web}} - \bar{y}_{\text{phone}} = 0.02$$

::: fragment
$$s^2_{\text{phone}} = 0.244; n_{\text{phone}} =1,778$$
:::

::: fragment
$$s^2_{\text{web}} =  0.246; n_{\text{web}} =2,066$$
:::

::: fragment
$$SE_{\bar{y}_{\text{web}} - \bar{y}_{\text{phone}}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.244}{1,778} + \frac{0.246}{2,066}} = 0.016$$
:::

### Confidence intervals for a difference

From here, we can calculate the 95% margin of error using the same strategy we used for a confidence interval $\text{SE}_\text{diff} \times 1.96 = 0.031$

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3

mean.1 <-0.00
sd.1 <- 0.016
zstart <- 2
zend <- 3
zcritical <- 1.65

my_col <- "#00998a"
x <- seq(from = mean.1 - 3*sd.1, to = mean.1 + 3*sd.1, by = .001)
MyDF <- data.frame(x = x, y = dnorm(x, mean = mean.1, sd = sd.1))

shade_curve <- function(MyDF, zstart, zend, fill = "red", alpha = .5){
  geom_area(data = subset(MyDF, x >= mean.1 + zstart*sd.1
                          & x < mean.1 + zend*sd.1),
            aes(y=y), fill = fill, color = NA, alpha = alpha)
}

ggplot(MyDF, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_line() +
  shade_curve(MyDF = MyDF, zstart = -1.96, zend = 1.96, fill = my_col, alpha = .3) +
  ylab("Density") +
  xlab("Errors") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.0, y = 1.5, label = "95%") + 
  geom_segment(aes(x=sd.1 * 1.96, y = 0, yend=5), lty=2) +
  geom_segment(aes(x=-sd.1 * 1.96, y = 0, yend=5), lty=2) +
  annotate("text", x=-sd.1 * 1.96, y = 9,  label = -1* round(sd.1* 1.96, digits=3)) +
  annotate("text", x=sd.1* 1.96, y = 9,  label = round(sd.1* 1.96, digits=3))





```

### Confidence intervals for a difference

Adding/Subtracting this range around our point estimate gives us a 95% confidence interval for the effect of Web vs. Phone surveys: \[-0.01,0.51\]

### Confidence intervals for a difference

We are 95% confident that the effect of web vs. phone surveys is between -1% and +5%

```{r}
#| fig-height: 1

mu<-0.02
sd<-0.016

df<-data.frame(
  estimate = "",
  mu  = mu, 
           ub =  mu + sd * 1.96,
           lb = mu - sd * 1.96)

ggplot(df, aes(x=mu, y=estimate, xmin=lb, xmax=ub)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbarh(height=0.2) +
  xlim(mu- sd * 3, mu+  sd * 3) +
  ylab("") +
  xlab("") +
  xlab("Estimated effect of Web vs. Phone on proportion approving Trump") +
  ylab("")


```

### Confidence intervals for a difference

Note that this range includes a negative effect, *and* a positive effect *and* no effect at all.

```{r}

```

### P values for a difference

**P values** are just an alternative method for conveying this same basic idea. A p-value represents the probability of seeing a result at least as large as the one in our sample if a null hypothesis is true.

::: fragment
In this case, our null hypothesis would typically be "there is no difference between web respondents vs. phone respondents"
:::

### P values for a difference

Assuming the actual effect of phone vs. web is zero, how often would this process give us an absolute difference in Trump support \>= 0.02?

### P values for a difference

This amounts to summing up the area in the two shaded regions of the sampling distribution when the difference is 0:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3

mean.1 <-0.00
sd.1 <- 0.016
zstart <- 2
zend <- 3
zcritical <- 1.65

my_col <- "#00998a"
x <- seq(from = mean.1 - 3*sd.1, to = mean.1 + 3*sd.1, by = .001)
MyDF <- data.frame(x = x, y = dnorm(x, mean = mean.1, sd = sd.1))

shade_curve <- function(MyDF, zstart, zend, fill = "red", alpha = .5){
  geom_area(data = subset(MyDF, x >= mean.1 + zstart*sd.1
                          & x < mean.1 + zend*sd.1),
            aes(y=y), fill = fill, color = NA, alpha = alpha)
}

ggplot(MyDF, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_line() +
  shade_curve(MyDF = MyDF, zstart = -5, zend =-0.02/0.016, fill = my_col, alpha = .3) +
  shade_curve(MyDF = MyDF, zstart = 0.02/0.016, zend =5, fill = my_col, alpha = .3) +

  ylab("Density") +
  xlab("Sampling Distribution under the null") +
 # annotate("text", x = 0.0, y = 1.5, label = "95%") + 
  geom_segment(aes(x=0.0195, y = 0, yend=20), lty=2) +
  geom_segment(aes(x=-0.021, y = 0, yend=20), lty=2) +
  annotate("text", x=-0.021, y = 22,  label = -0.02) +
  annotate("text", x=0.0195, y = 22,  label = 0.02)





```

      mean=0, 
      sd= 0.016, 
      lower.tail=F)

::: fragment
There is about a 21% chance of getting a difference equal to or absolutely greater than 0.02 if the effect is actually zero.
:::

### P values for a difference

By *convention* p-values less than or equal to .05 are considered *statistically significant*

::: fragment
Both p-value and confidence intervals are based on the same math, and "significance" under a 95% confidence interval also means "significance" under a (two-tailed) p-value.
:::

### Looking for Shy Trump Supporters

So what does this mean, and how do we know it?

### Looking for Shy Trump Supporters

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}
-   It means that we could rule out the possibility of "no effect" in four out of the 27 questions.
-   We know if because of what we can infer about the sampling distribution of the differences.

### Notes

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}

- P-values, confidence intervals, and statistical significance will come up again in this course. 
- This same basic framework can be applied to a lot of different kinds of statistical tests, not just comparing means or proportions.
- Keep in mind that these only address random sampling error, not any of the other kinds of error we might encounter.

:::

# Nuance! {background-color="#23373B"}

## Statistical Insignificance

The results here don't entirely rule out the possibility of a "Shy trump" supporter effect. There are really two reasons we might fail to find an effect:

-   There's actually no effect.
-   Not enough observations/too much variability to detect an effect/random chance.

## Statistical Insignificance

How large would the effect need to be for Pew's method to catch it?

$$
\frac{\text{Web vs. Phone}}{SE_\text{Web-Phone}}
$$

## Statistical Insignificance

How large would the effect need to be for Pew's study to find a significant result?

$$
\frac{\text{Effect}}{0.016} = 1.96
$$

::: fragment
At this sample size/standard error, the effect would need to be a little over $\pm3\%$ to be significant.

$$
1.96 \times 0.016 = 0.03136
$$
:::

## Statistical Insignificance

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}
-   On the other hand, Pew asked multiple questions about views on Trump, and none of them showed significant mode differences.
-   Other analyses of this phenomenon were also unable to find significant effects. [@Dropp2016; @coppock2017did]
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../images/pew_shytrump_other.png)
:::
::::::

## Complex Surveys and Design Effects

-   Pew recruited respondents using a complex sampling method, and responses were weighted to be more representative of the U.S. population.

-   These methods should make us more uncertain about the results.

## Design Effects

[Design effects]{.highlight} are one way to quantify the additional uncertainty introduced by a complex sampling method. The design effect is the ratio of the variance under a complex design compared to the variance you would get from a simple random sample.

## Design Effects

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Pew reports their design effect is 2.99, so our variance should be approximately 3 times larger than what we initially calculated.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../images/deff_pew.png)
:::
:::::

## Design Effects

Multiplying the variance by the design effect means that there's even more random sampling error expected here.

$$SE_{\bar{y}_{\text{web}} - \bar{y}_{\text{phone}}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.244}{1,778} + \frac{0.246}{2,066}} \times \sqrt{2.99} = 0.028 $$

::: fragment
$$\text{This difference is }\frac{0.02}{0.028} = .71 \text{ standard errors away from 0}$$
:::

::: fragment
This works out to around a p value of around .47, well above the conventional threshold for significance.
:::

## Design Effects

We can also formulate this as a 95% confidence interval around the difference of means.

$$
0.02 \pm 0.028\times 1.96 = (-0.035,0.075)
$$
